routes.description: Establish that textual criticism can responsibly recover the New Testament's wording in its essential substance by combining the surviving witness tradition, methods for comparing its readings, and a probabilistic standard appropriate to ancient historical evidence.
routes.successCriteria: Show that branching and abundant attestation preserves access to earlier readings, that most variation does not materially obstruct reconstruction, and that remaining local uncertainty is compatible with enough confidence to trust the recovered text without claiming absolute certainty.

motionBridge.description: Connect substantial recovery in essential respects, under a moderate historical-probability standard, to warranted trust in the New Testament text despite unresolved local readings.

centralBridges.description: Establish that manuscripts, early versions, patristic citations, and branching lines of transmission preserve sufficient comparative evidence to reconstruct readings rather than merely document cumulative corruption.
Distinguish the raw number of variants from the smaller burden-relevant class of meaningful and viable alternatives, while accounting for genuinely disputed passages.
Establish that the authors' wording is ordinarily represented among surviving readings and that critical comparison can identify it with substantial, though not exceptionless, confidence.
Justify a standard of responsible historical probability rather than certainty and show that the cumulative textual evidence meets that standard for substantial recovery.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how the limited effect of viable variants on essential claims supports practical textual trust without treating doctrinal stability as proof of every original reading.
Show that ordinary authorship, redactional, and textual scholarship coherently depends on sufficiently stable wording and therefore supplies a practical check on sweeping unrecoverability claims.

routes.description: Establish that reconstruction of the earliest text represented by surviving witnesses does not by itself warrant confidence that this text is the authors' wording, because the decisive early transmission period is undocumented and may contain consequential alterations no extant comparison can reveal.
routes.successCriteria: Show that evidence drawn from surviving witnesses cannot resolve the accuracy of their lost ancestors, that some consequential readings remain disputed or unknowable, and that comparative abundance or broad continuity therefore falls short of the affirmative burden to justify textual trust.

motionBridge.description: Connect unresolved uncertainty about pre-survival transmission and consequential original readings to the failure of the available evidence to warrant enough confidence for textual trust.

centralBridges.description: Establish that the gap between composition and the earliest useful witnesses leaves the competence, exemplars, and alterations of the earliest copyists beyond direct comparison.
Maintain the distinction between reconstructing the common ancestor of surviving witnesses and establishing that this reconstructed initial text is identical with an author's wording.
Show that counts and proportions derived from surviving variants cannot measure consequential omissions or alterations that arose before the ancestry represented by extant witnesses.
Establish that intentional changes, substantial variants, and permanently disputed readings matter historically and textually even when they do not overturn an essential doctrine.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish the comparative ease supplied by numerous manuscripts from proof that their reconstructable ancestry preserves the autograph rather than an already altered text.
Identify the missing early, independent, closely dated controls that would connect surviving textual agreement to the authors' wording with stronger evidential warrant.

sections.title: Early Transmission and the Surviving Witness Base
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the lost early copying period is adequately controlled by the abundance, age, independence, and branching character of manuscripts, versions, and patristic witnesses.

sections.title: Scale, Viability, and Significance of Textual Variants
sections.rationale: This issue distinguishes raw variant totals and ordinary copying errors from meaningful, viable, intentional, or otherwise consequential differences relevant to substantial recovery.

sections.title: Initial Text, Extant Readings, and the Autographs
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether reconstructing readings represented in the surviving tradition warrants identifying the resulting initial text with the authors' wording.

sections.title: Evidentiary Standard, Probability, and Burden of Trust
sections.rationale: This issue determines what degree of historical probability the motion requires and whether indirect evidence and residual uncertainty satisfy or defeat that burden.

sections.title: Doctrinal, Historical, and Scholarly Consequences
sections.rationale: This issue examines how doctrinal stability, historically important differences, and scholarly reliance on stable wording bear on practical textual trust without substituting for autographic proof.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The centuries and unknown copying stages between the New Testament originals and the earliest useful surviving witnesses leave changes introduced during early transmission unknowable.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Ehrman's uninterrupted opening statement after his explicit introduction by the moderator.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly establishes the evidentiary gap during the earliest transmission period and therefore needs no opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly develops a central premise with a concrete chronological comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is recoverable, though references to what cannot be known compress the distinction between particular unknown changes and total transmission knowledge.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Missing early manuscripts warrants substantial uncertainty, but the categorical inability to know slightly exceeds what absence of direct copies alone establishes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from absent early controls to unresolved early changes is strong, with a bounded bridge from direct absence to unknowability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The chronology and missing-copy comparison specifically support the gap, though indirect evidence and manuscript ancestry are not comparatively assessed.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman

evidenceWarrant.rationale: P45 and the fragment chronology offer specific support, but the broader distribution and ancestry claims are only compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary abundance distinction but does not itself complete the central lost-transmission bridge.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Although most textual variants are insignificant, intentional and consequential differences affect prominent passages and disputed wording concerning theology, narrative, and the portrayal of Jesus.
moves.attributionBasis: The examples are delivered continuously by Ehrman during the opening argument following his explicit introduction as the first speaker.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Luke 22 and the adulterous-woman narrative provide concrete support, though representativeness across the corpus is not established.

moves.speaker: Daniel B. Wallace
moves.proposition: Identifying scribal corruption presupposes that the earlier wording can be distinguished among manuscript readings, and scholarship on textual tampering routinely assumes that the autographic wording remains available there.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker remains Wallace, and he explicitly invokes Ehrman's scholarly work as support for this inference.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether absent early copies make the authors' wording inaccessible rather than merely less directly evidenced.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the accessibility demand by arguing that identifying corruption in detailed scholarship presupposes recoverable prior wording, though it does not prove that every such judgment reaches the autograph.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer contacting the decisive accessibility inference but leaving the autograph-identification bridge materially compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The inference is clear, but earlier text, initial text, and autographic wording are treated too readily as equivalent across the cited scholarship.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Detecting a later alteration requires a prior comparative reading, but it does not necessarily establish that the identified reading is autographic.

charity.alternative: Ehrman's corruption judgments can identify changes relative to an earlier reconstructable text without claiming direct access to every autograph.

moves.speaker: Daniel B. Wallace

A further demand concerns whether nonmanuscript witnesses materially constrain otherwise undocumented early transmission.

moves.proposition: Essential Christian beliefs do not depend on textually suspect passages and are not overturned by viable textual variants, even though particular passages may remain disputed.
moves.attributionBasis: Wallace introduces the theological-dependence question and attributes the supporting concession directly to Ehrman's published response.

moves.speaker: Daniel B. Wallace
moves.proposition: The standard critical Greek text lists tens of thousands of variants but only a small set of places where scholars have proposed that no Greek manuscript preserves the original wording, indicating that the autographic reading ordinarily survives among extant alternatives.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted argument continues Wallace's identified presentation and uses his affirmative position on textual recoverability.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether lost early transmission plausibly removed the authors' wording from all surviving alternatives.
A related demand is whether the surviving tradition retains original readings despite the lateness of most witnesses.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument provides meaningful contrary evidence but omits the strongest qualification concerning undetectable pre-survival changes.

moves.speaker: Daniel B. Wallace
moves.proposition: Detailed New Testament scholarship, including vocabulary-based authorship analysis, routinely presupposes dependable knowledge of the wording across nearly every passage relevant to its conclusions.
moves.attributionBasis: Wallace explicitly discusses Ehrman and Ehrman's publications from the standpoint of the affirmative debater's ongoing presentation.

components.text: The contacted demand is whether sweeping textual unknowability coheres with detailed scholarship that relies on stable wording.

response.rationale: The reply supplies a practical consistency check against total skepticism, but it does not directly establish that scholarly working texts equal the autographs.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts a practical implication of skepticism while leaving the decisive early-evidence demand unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: Stable wording, recovered wording, and autographic wording are insufficiently separated, and the scope of scholarship requiring exact wording is broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Scholarly practice supports substantial stability, but it need not presuppose autographic certainty at every passage relevant to an argument.

charity.alternative: Scholars can conduct authorship and redaction analysis using critically reconstructed wording while retaining uncertainty about autographic identity.
charity.decisiveQualification: Practical reliance supports sufficient local stability but does not prove the autograph at every relevant locus.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: A small proportion of meaningful and viable variants among surviving manuscripts cannot measure significant omissions, editions, or alterations introduced before the earliest extant witnesses.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Ehrman's announced response and directly challenges a numerical claim attributed to Wallace's preceding presentation.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether percentages calculated from extant variants can measure alterations predating the surviving manuscript ancestry.
The raw insignificance percentage also depends on the extant observed variant set.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: A textual difference or loss can be historically and textually important even if it alters no essential Christian doctrine, so doctrinal stability is not a sufficient measure of significance.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman's response explicitly grants the theological point attributed to Wallace and then supplies his own counterexample and criterion of significance.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether preservation of essential doctrines is the proper criterion for assessing textual and historical significance.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Confidence in the New Testament text requires evidence that the earliest surviving copies descend from accurate predecessors rather than from significantly altered exemplars.
